GitHub Copilot CLI: request flow and controls

The step-by-step guide explains each step in general; how to read these trees.

What happens to a request

The steps run in the typical order. A documented order, where the vendor states one, is shown on its step. A decision point appears where the documentation describes a real branch; an agent with none has none documented.

A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

  1. Choose the front door ◐ documented, with limits !

    You can use it in a terminal, from an editor, in a desktop app, from scripts, in automated workflows or through a pull request comment. The documentation says scripted runs cannot use the cloud sandbox.

  2. Apply organization rules ● documented !

    Companies can push settings that load before yours, switch off features such as computer use, and limit which models people may pick. A repository can also list the built-in models it allows.

    Documented order: Settings pushed through a device management system load before the user's own settings.

  3. Load the house rules ◐ documented, with limits !

    It reads instruction files from the repository and your home folder and combines them rather than picking one. The documentation disagrees on absolute paths in imports, and a helper agent does not follow the repository's instructions by default.

    Documented order: Personal instructions rank highest, then repository, then organization, though all sets are provided.

  4. Load memory and earlier sessions ◐ documented, with limits !

    It can remember facts about your repository, resume or fork earlier sessions, and hand a session between GitHub and your machine. Resuming cannot be combined with a workflow run, and picker screens are not handled by the editor protocol.

  5. Stock the built-in tools ● documented !

    It starts with a small set of built-in tools to search, read and edit files, run shell commands and fetch web pages. Shell commands run directly on your machine until you turn on the local sandbox, and web addresses need approval by default.

  6. Load skills and custom commands ◐ documented, with limits !

    A skill is a folder of instructions the agent can use when a task fits, or you can call it by name. A command is a simple file, and a skill beats a command with the same name. A skill can pre-approve tools it names; Copilot asks about the rest.

    Decision point: Will a skill ask before it uses a tool?

    • The tool is on the skill's allowed list: The tool is allowed automatically while the skill is active.

      tools that are automatically allowed when the skill is active

    • The tool is not on the list: Copilot asks you for permission before using the tool.

      Copilot will prompt you for permission before using it

    Documented in F08.skill-overrides. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  7. Connect outside tools ◐ documented, with limits !

    It connects to outside tools through MCP, as local programs or remote servers, with GitHub's own server ready. You can allow or deny a whole server or one tool. The documentation names one config file for a single setting and does not give a full list of places.

  8. Set the safety posture ◐ documented, with limits !

    It asks before risky actions and asks you to trust a folder. Plan and autopilot modes cycle with a key, and a bypass option skips the questions. The documentation disagrees on how many modes exist and whether autopilot stays on, and does not name the starting mode.

    Documented order: A rule that denies a tool takes precedence over the allow options.

    Decision point: If I allow a tool but a rule denies it, which wins?

    • Allowed with a command-line allow option: The deny option takes precedence over the allow options.

      --deny-tool takes precedence over --allow-all-tools and --allow-tool

    • Approved automatically or saved earlier: A rule that denies the tool takes precedence over those approvals.

      permission rules that deny a tool take precedence over automatic or saved approvals

    Documented in F04.config-scope-precedence. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  9. Pick the model and thinking effort ◐ documented, with limits

    You can pick the model and thinking effort in a session, at startup or in a settings file, or use your own model provider. Enterprise rules limit which models appear, the research helper keeps its own model, and the settings file list of effort levels leaves out max.

    Documented order: A repository effort setting that pins the default takes precedence over the user value.

  10. Prepare an isolated workspace ● documented

    It can create a separate Git worktree and switch to it, leaving your uncommitted changes behind, or fork a session into a new worktree. A setting can start new worktrees from the remote default branch.

B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

  1. Assemble the prompt ● documented !

    The latest models support a very large context window, and you can choose a default or longer size. Naming a file adds it to the prompt, organization exclusion rules are respected, and large tool output is saved to a file with a preview sent to the model.

    Documented order: A repository context size setting pins the default tier and takes precedence.

  2. Run your own code at set moments ◔ partly documented !

    Hooks are shell commands that run at points such as session start or before a tool runs, and can allow or deny a tool call. The documentation does not mention matcher rules for choosing which tools a hook covers. A setting can turn hooks off.

    Decision point: When do repository hooks run in one-off prompt mode?

    • The prompt-mode hooks variable is set to true: Repository hooks load in prompt mode.

      Repository hooks load in prompt mode (-p) when GITHUB_COPILOT_PROMPT_MODE_REPO_HOOKS is set to true

    • The folder is trusted or allow-all is set: Repository hooks also load automatically.

      also load automatically when the folder is already trusted or COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL is set

    • The user setting that disables hooks is on: Both repository-level and user-level hooks are disabled.

      A user setting can disable all hooks, both repository-level and user-level

    Documented in F06.trust-enable. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

  1. Send the request and handle trouble ◐ documented, with limits

    Auto mode picks a model from system health, performance and task difficulty, and you can ask for a tier. When a setting is on, a rate limit error switches to auto mode and retries, but not for global limits or your own provider. Included credits reset monthly.

  2. Set the thinking budget ◐ documented, with limits

    Some models offer a choice of reasoning depth, and the documentation does not list the levels per model. A key shows or hides the model's reasoning. Summaries appear for supporting OpenAI models, and the documentation does not describe a token budget control.

  3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt · not researched not yet researched

D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

  1. Read what the model asked for · not researched not yet researched
  2. Decide whether it is allowed ◐ documented, with limits !

    Rules can allow or deny tools, folders and shell commands by name. Command matching is literal, with no regular expressions or general wildcards. Assisted approval still asks each time but adds a model's safety recommendation, so the CLI can approve requests it judges acceptable.

  3. Save an undo point ● documented

    It tracks the file changes it makes for each prompt. Pressing the escape key twice while it is idle rewinds the session to an earlier prompt and can restore your files.

  4. Run it inside the fence ◐ documented, with limits !

    Shell commands and searches can run in a local sandbox that limits where they write and whether they reach the network. It is experimental. File tools follow it on a best-effort basis, remote MCP servers stay outside it, and enterprise settings can require it.

    Decision point: Can I switch the sandbox off for a session?

    • The effective policy permits sandbox bypass: You can turn sandboxing off for the rest of the current session.

      a user can explicitly disable sandboxing for the rest of the current session

    • Enterprise managed settings require sandboxing: Ordinary configuration and the no-sandbox startup option do not switch it off.

      If enterprise managed settings require sandboxing

    Documented in F05.sandbox-override. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Tidy the tool's output · not researched not yet researched
  6. Feed the result back and go round again ◐ documented, with limits !

    It works through a prompt in rounds of model reply and tool use, and a prompt you send while it is thinking is treated as steering. In autopilot a setting caps the follow-on messages, and the documentation disagrees on the default.

  7. Hand work to helpers ◐ documented, with limits !

    Custom helper agents are described in Markdown files with their own tools, and can have their own model and effort. Several run at once under limits on depth and number. The documentation disagrees on the default depth and cap, and the research helper uses a fixed model.

    Documented order: For helper effort, a per-call value wins, then a settings override, then the agent's own definition.

    Decision point: Which model does a helper agent use?

    • Its agent profile names a model: The helper runs on the model named in that profile.

      that model is used by the subagent

    • It is the built-in research agent: It uses a fixed model that the model command does not change.

      The built-in research agent is hard-coded to use a particular AI model

    Documented in F09.per-agent-model. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  8. Shrink the context when it fills ◐ documented, with limits

    It summarizes older conversation automatically, or you can ask for it by hand and add focus instructions. A finished compaction cannot be undone. The documentation disagrees on when the automatic step starts: about 80 percent in two places, 95 percent in another.

  9. Show the answer or ask you ◐ documented, with limits

    Plan mode lets you work out a plan before code is written, and remote clients can approve or reject it. The plan description does not call plan mode read-only. The terminal shows the model used for each response and whether sandboxing is on.

  10. Wrap up and keep score ◐ documented, with limits !

    It shows context use and AI credits spent in a session, can cap spending per response, and can export telemetry in a standard monitoring format. The spending cap is a soft limit, and user budgets are not considered when the organization is billed directly.

E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

  1. Run without you watching ● documented !

    It can run tasks in the background, repeat or delay a prompt on a schedule, hand work to a cloud agent on GitHub, and be watched or steered from GitHub or GitHub Mobile. Automations react to events such as an issue being opened and skip people without write access by default.

  2. Extend and share ◐ documented, with limits !

    A plugin bundles skills, hooks, helper agents and MCP servers, and installs from a repository, a marketplace or a local folder. Installed plugins are cached, so local changes need a reinstall. Auto-update works only in your own or managed settings, not a repository's.

    Documented order: When a policy pins a plugin or marketplace, the managed value wins over local changes.

  3. Updates and releases ● documented !

    It can check its version, update itself, show its changelog with an optional summary, and turn automatic updates off for CI. Some features need an experimental switch, and the documentation lists retired models and removed options.

  4. Where it runs and who runs it ◐ documented, with limits

    It is part of GitHub Copilot: the Copilot app is built on it, and it runs in a JetBrains terminal. It needs a Copilot seat unless you bring your own model provider, and delegating needs a sign-in. Pull requests need a Git repository on GitHub; operating systems are not listed.

    Decision point: Do I need a GitHub account to use it?

    • You use GitHub-hosted models: You need an assigned Copilot seat, and each interaction uses AI credits.

      Access to Copilot CLI requires an assigned GitHub Copilot seat

    • You bring your own model provider: It can connect to your provider without a GitHub account or token.

      With BYOK, Copilot CLI can connect to the configured provider without a GitHub account or token

    Documented in F21.shared-account-billing. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Identity, retention and audit ◐ documented, with limits !

    Users need a Copilot seat and sign in through GitHub, and a list of approved organizations can pin who may sign in. Policy changes appear in the audit log. Anthropic keeps prompts for some Claude models by default, with zero retention on request under a time-bound exemption.
